allowedClaimsDebtDeltas.before:
450 psi against what, exactly?

Water pressure sounds dramatic, but it’s modest: about 0.43 psi per foot of depth. Eight feet of groundwater pushes about 3.5 psi at the base of a wall, whether it’s a soaked yard or a lake. Only depth matters.

Water pressure at the base of an 8 ft wall~3.5 psi
WetBond pull-off test450 psi

A steel disc glued to the treated surface was pulled straight off. The concrete tore at 450 psi before the bond let go, so the bond is at least that strong.

Coatings rarely fail from that push. They fail because vapor and crystallizing minerals keep lifting them from behind. WetBond is embedded 0.7 to 1 inch inside the concrete, so there’s no film to lift. A pull test isn’t a water-pressure rating; that test is under way. Water rising under the floor is a separate check your dealer makes. The science

allowedClaimsDebtDeltas.before:
More than a decade in the field

WetBond is a new name. The chemistry isn't.

Before WetBond, the same water-reactive chemistry family was working on wet concrete in commercial and infrastructure jobs. A few milestones:

Circa 2010Publicly described as a primer that penetrates wet concrete and forms a three-dimensional water block.
Circa 2010Saved a retail slab emitting more than twice the moisture conventional coatings tolerate. The case study is below.
2021Selected as one of two top performers in an Ohio DOT and University of Cincinnati bridge study (report FHWA/OH-2021-13).
TodaySold as WetBond, applied by trained applicators and Certified Dealers.
Retail · sporting goods chain · 8,000 sq ft · circa 2010

A slab too wet to coat, finished in time for opening.

The problem
A new store needed a clear two-coat floor finish three weeks before its grand opening. The slab had been poured months earlier and should have dried. It hadn't: testing showed a moisture vapor emission rate of 8.4 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours, where conventional floor coatings fail at about 3.4.
The complication
Nylon fibers in the concrete melted onto the diamond grinding pads, fouling them almost immediately.
The fix
The crew ground with an emulsifying solution to control the fibers, then primed with a water-reactive grade from the WetBond chemistry family, built to bond to damp concrete.
The result
The floor was finished and handed over in time for the grand opening.

Field history of the chemistry family behind WetBond, circa 2010. The job predates the WetBond name. Moisture figures are vapor emission rates from a calcium chloride test.

Healthcare · hospital kitchen · circa 2010

Surface films peel. Here's what replaced one.

The problem
The kitchen's epoxy floor was delaminating. The kitchen ran around the clock, so it couldn't close, and the hospital banned solvent-based products and anything that off-gassed.
The approach
Crews worked off-hours, one half of the kitchen at a time, with the area tented and grinding dust captured by HEPA filtration.
The system
Damaged areas were repaired with a self-leveling filler, then a three-coat, 100% solids, zero-VOC polyurea floor system went down with non-skid aggregate and a 12-inch cove base.
The result
Both halves were finished within the allowed window, with no solvent odor in the hospital.
